steps.prompt: What is a game, under the hood?
steps.sub: It's one tiny cycle run dozens of times a second: read input, update the world, draw the frame. By the end you'll name your game's core verb and trace one frame through the loop.

steps.prompt: What's the 'core mechanic' of a game?

options.t: The menu screen and the settings panel.
The one central action the whole game is built around — the verb you do over and over.
The list of credits at the end.

steps.why: A core mechanic is a verb: jump, shoot, stack, match, dodge. Tetris is 'rotate-and-drop'. Flappy Bird is 'flap'. It's the action you repeat constantly — everything else (menus, score, art) is built around it.
hints: Think of one word the player DOES again and again.
Menus and credits aren't the thing you actually play.

steps.prompt: Every frame, the game runs this same little cycle.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This three-step loop is the heartbeat of every game.

cards.b: Read what the player is doing right now — a key held, a screen tapped, a stick pushed.
Change the world: move the character, check collisions, apply gravity, update the score.
Draw the new state to the screen — one frame. Then it all repeats, 30–60 times a second.

steps.prompt: Tap the three stages in the order they run each frame.
steps.sub: This order repeats every single frame.
hints: You can't move the character before you know what the player pressed.
Read → change → draw. Drawing is always last.

steps.prompt: Why read input and update FIRST, and render LAST — every frame?
steps.sub: Think about what would look wrong if you flipped it.

options.t: It's just tradition; the order doesn't matter.
You must know the new state before you draw it, or the frame shows stale, last-frame positions.
Rendering is the slowest part, so it has to go first to warm up.

steps.why: Render shows the current state. If you draw before updating, the player presses 'right' but sees the character where it was last frame — input feels laggy and broken. Read input, move the world, THEN draw the result. That's why render is last.
hints: What does 'render' actually draw — the old positions or the new ones?
If you draw before you move, the screen is always one frame behind.

steps.prompt: Sort each line of game code into its loop stage.
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap the stage it belongs to.

items.t: Check if the right-arrow key is held
Move the player 5 units to the right
Apply gravity so the player falls
Read the touch position on screen
Draw the player sprite at its new spot

hints: Reading a key or a touch is Input. Drawing pixels is Render.
Moving, falling, colliding — anything that CHANGES the world — is Update.

steps.prompt: Walk one frame of a simple runner. Player is holding 'right' and there's a wall ahead.
steps.sub: At each turn, pick what the loop does next. The frame log fills in.
steps.goal: Process one frame correctly: read, update, draw.

turns.situation: A new frame begins. The player is holding the right-arrow key.
turns.q: What does the loop do first?
options: Read input → note that 'right' is held

turns.situation: Input is read. The player wants to move right, but there's a wall 2 units ahead.
options: Move right, but the collision check stops the player at the wall
Draw the wall and the player
turns.log: ⚙️ Update → tried +5 right, collision clamps player to the wall.

turns.situation: The world state is now updated: player is pressed against the wall.
turns.q: What's the final stage of this frame?
options: Render → draw the player at the wall
turns.log: 🖼️ Render → frame drawn with player at the wall.

turns.situation: The frame is done and drawn.
options: Loop back → start the next frame with Input again
Skip input for the next 100 frames
turns.log: 🔁 Next frame begins → Input → Update → Render, again.

hints: The loop is always Input → Update → Render, then it repeats.
Collision is part of Update — it changes the world before anything is drawn.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: The game loop runs once when the game starts, then stops.
statements.why: No — it runs continuously, many times a second, for as long as the game is playing. One run = one frame.

statements.t: Movement code (read keys, change position) belongs in the per-frame update.
statements.why: Right — movement is read-input-then-update, and it has to happen every frame so the character responds in real time.

statements.t: A solid core mechanic is usually one repeatable verb, not a dozen unrelated systems.
statements.why: Yes — great small games nail ONE verb (flap, match, dodge) and build everything around it.

statements.t: On a phone, the loop disappears — touch games don't have a game loop.
statements.why: No — same loop. Only the INPUT stage changes: it reads touches instead of keys. Update and render are identical.

hints: Picture the runner trace — did the loop run once or every frame?
Keyboard vs touch only swaps what Input reads; the loop stays the same.

steps.sub: Not graded. Pin down the heartbeat of YOUR game.

fields.label: In one verb, what's your game's core mechanic?
What input drives it on keyboard AND on touch?
fields.ph: e.g. arrow keys on PC, swipe left/right on phone

steps.prompt: Tap EVERYTHING that happens inside the per-frame Update stage.
steps.sub: Some of these belong to other stages or run only once. Pick only the per-frame Update work.
chips: Show the studio logo on launch
steps.why: Update is where the WORLD changes each frame: movement, gravity, collisions, score. Drawing the frame is Render, and the studio logo on launch happens once at startup — neither is per-frame Update.
hints: Update = changing the world state. What's the odd one that draws pixels?
A launch logo happens once, not every frame.
